```{r}
#| label: obx-setup

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

#
# YOUR OWN TABLE STYLES, PAGE 6 (S422 review; was Publication tables page
# 10). It uses page 4's route (Jeff, S421: "the
# example prompt, naming the sections, the list of what could not be matched
# read as a start, the look and not the typesetting, published examples only;

#

#
# S431 (Jeff's S429 read of the Publication tables pages, okayed): the Word

# HOW-TO LAYOUT (S344). No top boxes: the shared material lives once on

#

# changes A-M and the page's 16 numbered changes; the request text in block 3
# is the S418 test's prompt, left as it was.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

options(width = 80)   # match a default 80-column console for table alignment
options(jstats.attach.noninteractive = TRUE)   # let block 1 show the real startup message

# THE SHARED LIST (S422): every Publication tables page's files, so a render
# halted on one page cannot leave a style file in the Styles folder another
# page creates and lists. A Styles folder still holding anything else HALTS
# the render: it is not this page's to remove.
.tables_files <- c("Styles/myreport.jstyle", "Styles/mystyle.jstyle",
                   "Styles/myblue.jstyle", "Styles/mytest.txt",
                   "Styles/mytest.jstyle", "Styles/mymatch.jstyle",
                   "myblue.txt", "mymatch.txt",
                   file.path("Tables", c("Descriptives.docx",
                     "Regression.docx", "Tables.docx", "Tables_v2.docx",
                     "Table1_mystyle.docx", "Table1_report.docx",
                     "Table1_myblue.docx", "Tables_mymatch.docx",
                     "Models.docx")))
.mt_clean <- function() {
  f <- .tables_files[file.exists(.tables_files)]
  if (length(f)) file.remove(f)
  if (dir.exists("Styles") &&
      !length(list.files("Styles", all.files = TRUE, no.. = TRUE)))
    unlink("Styles", recursive = TRUE)
  if (dir.exists("Tables") &&
      !length(list.files("Tables", all.files = TRUE, no.. = TRUE)))
    unlink("Tables", recursive = TRUE)
  invisible(NULL)
}
.mt_clean()
if (dir.exists("Styles"))
  stop("The project's Styles folder holds files no Publication tables page ",
       "wrote. Move them out and render again.", call. = FALSE)

source("pane_facsimile.R")   # defines .obx (dot-named); turns the output color on
```

## Matching the look of a published table

**Your own table styles &middot; Page 6**\
*This page uses the route of
[4. Changing a style with an AI assistant](tables-ai-assistant.qmd), so read
that page first.*

Instead of describing a look to an AI assistant, you can show the assistant an
example: attach a published table that you'd like your tables to look like,
along with a copy of a jstats style, and ask the assistant to change the style
to match. This page is a
hands-on run-through of that request, and of what to check in the reply.

The steps are page 4's, with an example attached: a copy of a style and a copy
to upload, the request, the check with `jstyle()`, and a table in the new
style. This page says less about each step than page 4 does, and more about
what is different when the request is an example.

This page follows the pattern of every How-To: numbered blocks of code that
build one script, with the finished script to download at the bottom.
[Using the How-To pages](howtos.qmd#using-the-how-to-pages) explains the
pattern, and how to reset your session if something goes wrong.

### 1. Load jstats and the data

We'll work on `community`, one of the two practice datasets that ship with the
package: 103 simulated respondents to a community survey. `jload()` puts a copy
of it in your workspace, and `juse()` makes `community` the default data frame,
so the commands that follow can leave its name out.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
.obx$show_console(r"---(## ---- 1. Load jstats and the data --------------------------------------

## Load jstats and the community practice dataset, and make community the
## default data frame. quiet = TRUE skips jload()'s report on what it
## loaded; overwrite = TRUE replaces a copy already loaded in this session
## without asking first
library(jstats)
jload("community", overwrite = TRUE, quiet = TRUE)
juse(community))---", fence = TRUE,
  lead = "The command lines are shown; the standalone <code>##</code> comment lines aren't -- running a comment just echoes it back and does nothing.")
```

```{r}
#| label: output-folder
#| include: false
# The output folder Publication tables page 2 sets, which this page assumes
# (its text says so where the Word file is written): set here out of sight, so
# the Word file and the summary's path are as that reader sees them. The
# teardown removes the folder when it is left empty.
invisible(joptions(output.dir = "Tables", quiet = TRUE))
```

### 2. A copy of report, and a copy to upload

Start from the built-in style that is closer to your example: `report` for an
agency's or an institute's report, `apa` for a journal that follows APA style. This page uses
`report`, saved as `mymatch`, and a copy of it named `mymatch.txt` for the
upload.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
.obx$show_console(r"---(## ---- 2. A copy of report, and a copy to upload ------------------------

## Keep this page's styles in a Styles folder inside the project
joptions(style.dir = "Styles")

## Save a complete copy of report as mymatch, every setting written out
## with a note
jstyle("report", save.as = "mymatch")

## file.copy() is base R: it copies a file. The copy, ending in .txt, is
## the one to upload
file.copy("Styles/mymatch.jstyle", "mymatch.txt", overwrite = TRUE)  # base R)---",
  fence = TRUE)
```

jstats wrote the copy, `mymatch.jstyle`, into the `Styles` folder, and
`file.copy()` answered `TRUE`: `mymatch.txt` is ready to upload.

### 3. Ask your assistant (outside R)

This step happens in your AI assistant, not in R. The block below is only
comments, a note in your script of what you did.

```r
## ---- 3. Ask your assistant (outside R) --------------------------------

## Upload mymatch.txt and the example with the request on the guide page,
## and save the file that comes back as mymatch.jstyle in the Styles
## folder, replacing the copy there
```

Open a new chat in your assistant, attach `mymatch.txt` and the example, here a
report saved as `Report.pdf`, and send this message, naming the kinds of table
you make:

```text
Attached are mymatch.txt, a jstats table style whose notes say what each
setting does and what it takes, and Report.pdf. Change the style file so that
jstats tables look like the tables in the report, following the instructions
at the top of the file. I make tables of descriptive statistics, regressions
and crosstabs: set each of their sections to match as well. Give me the
changed file as a download named mymatch.jstyle. Then list each value you
changed, old and new, and anything the settings cannot reproduce.
```

Save the file that comes back as `mymatch.jstyle` in the `Styles` folder,
replacing the copy there, as page 4 describes, and keep the assistant's reply.

Four things matter more here than with a request in words.

- **Name the kinds of table you make**, and ask the assistant to set each
  one's section. Each kind of table has a section of the style file to itself, and the
  sections decide much of a table's shape, such as which columns a regression
  table shows and which fit statistics go under it. In a test, an assistant
  asked only to match an article's tables changed fourteen general settings
  and no section.
- **Treat the assistant's list of what it couldn't match as a start.** In the
  same test the list missed differences that a section's settings could have
  removed. Compare your Word tables with the example yourself, in block 5.
- **Copy the look, not the typesetting.** A published table was set by a
  typesetter, and its font sizes and tight spacing suit the printed page. A
  manuscript follows the journal's guidelines for authors, which usually ask
  for something plainer.
- **Use only published examples.** A file you upload leaves your computer, so
  never upload a draft, unpublished results, or anything confidential.

So far this has been tried with a scanned journal article, with Microsoft
Copilot. A screenshot, or a PDF saved straight from a word processor, hasn't
been tried yet.

### 4. Check what came back

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
.b4 <- r"---(## ---- 4. Check what came back ------------------------------------------

## jstyle() reads the file and shows every setting. It stops at a line it
## cannot use, and names the line
jstyle("mymatch"))---"
cat(strrep("`", 3), "r\n", .b4, "\n", strrep("`", 3), "\n", sep = "")
```

What `jstyle()` shows depends on your example, so this page can't show it;
page 4 shows the list of settings and how to read it. Check the values that
changed against the assistant's list of changes. If `jstyle()` stops, give its message
to the assistant, ask it to fix that line, and check the file again.

### 5. One table of each kind, in one file

Then make a table of each kind you named, from results of your own or from the
practice data, and write the tables to one Word file to compare with the
example. As on
[Making a table in Word](tables-in-word.qmd), Publication tables page 2, this
assumes you've already set your output folder with
`joptions(output.dir = "Tables")`, so the Word file goes in `Tables`. To set the folder once for every session, put that line in
your project's `.Rprofile`, as
[Loading jstats automatically](loading-jstats-automatically.qmd) shows.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
.b5 <- r"---(## ---- 5. One table of each kind, in one file ---------------------------

## Save a result of each kind named in the request
d1 <- jdesc(Age, Income, WellbeingScore, print = FALSE)
m1 <- jlm(WellbeingScore ~ Age + Income, print = FALSE)
x1 <- jcrosstab(Volunteer ~ Region, print = FALSE)

## Make a table from each result in mymatch. list() is base R: it puts
## the three tables together, and jtable() writes them to one Word file
t1 <- jtable(d1, style = "mymatch")
t2 <- jtable(m1, style = "mymatch")
t3 <- jtable(x1, style = "mymatch")
jtable(list(t1, t2, t3), file = "Tables_mymatch.docx", open = TRUE))---"
cat(strrep("`", 3), "r\n", .b5, "\n", strrep("`", 3), "\n", sep = "")
```

```{r}
#| label: blocks-4-5
#| include: false
# Blocks 4 and 5 are plain fences (see the setup chunk); their code strings,
# printed as the fences above, run here on the unchanged copy, so the script
# runs and a line that stops halts the render.
.out4 <- gsub("\033\\[[0-9;]*m", "", utils::capture.output(eval(parse(text = .b4))))
.out5 <- utils::capture.output(eval(parse(text = .b5)))
```

Open the Word file beside the example and compare them table by table. For a
difference you'd like removed, ask the assistant about it in the same chat,
naming the table and what differs, and check the new file the same way.

## What a style can't match

A style changes only what its settings can change. Page 4's list,
[What a style can and can't do](tables-ai-assistant.qmd#what-a-style-can-and-cant-do),
gives the main limits. An example can show one more: a table laid out in a way
no jstats table is, such as regression models of different outcomes side by
side, which jstats makes only as separate tables. No change to a style
produces that layout.

```{r}
#| label: prose-gates
#| include: false

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# PROSE GATES -- hidden. Each stopifnot() below is one statement the prose
# makes about what the package does; a false one HALTS the render.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
.cp <- readLines("Styles/mymatch.jstyle", encoding = "UTF-8")
.sections <- sub("^\\[(.*)\\]$", "\\1", grep("^\\[[a-z]+\\]$", .cp, value = TRUE))
.td <- tempfile("mt-"); dir.create(.td)
.err <- function(expr) tryCatch({ expr; NA_character_ },
                                error = function(e) conditionMessage(e))
# models of different outcomes stop: separate tables only
.m_other <- jlm(Age ~ Income, print = FALSE)
.e_two <- .err(jtable(list(m1, .m_other)))
stopifnot(
  # block 2: the copy, and the upload copy
  file.exists("Styles/mymatch.jstyle"), file.exists("mymatch.txt"),
  identical(readLines("mymatch.txt"), .cp),
  # the request names three kinds of table, each a section of the file
  all(c("descriptives", "regression", "crosstab") %in% .sections),
  # blocks 4 and 5 ran: the style read, three tables in one file
  any(grepl("^Style: mymatch", .out4)),
  file.exists(file.path("Tables", "Tables_mymatch.docx")), !file.exists("Tables_mymatch.docx"),
  any(grepl("3 tables written to", .out5, fixed = TRUE)),
  # models of different outcomes: no one table
  !is.na(.e_two)
)
unlink(.td, recursive = TRUE)
```

## Take the whole script with you

That's the full run-through. If you'd like the entire script in one file to
keep and reuse, download it here. Put your own results in place of `d1`, `m1`,
and `x1`, and your own style's name in place of `mymatch`.

The file is the finished version of the script you built: the same code, in the
same order. Block 3 is still only comments: the assistant's part happens
outside R. If you run the file again, jstats asks before replacing each file it
wrote earlier; the file's first lines say what to answer.
[Using the How-To pages](howtos.qmd#using-the-how-to-pages) says more about
finished scripts and how to run one.
